name: user_roles
description: A role assignment: this account holds this role, as far as user_role_scopes reaches. One row per assignment, and the same role may be assigned twice with different scopes. An account with no row here is a USER — the table lists the exceptions, not the members.

columns.name: role
columns.description: A RoleNames value or a roles.name — resolved in that order, so a default role can never be shadowed by a created one. A name that is neither is ignored with a warning, never rejected. Not a foreign key: the default roles have no row to point at, and they are the majority of what this column holds.

notes: No row means USER. That is why the table stays small enough to be read per session on the miss path: only moderators, admins and the holders of created roles have rows at all. An implementation that treats a missing row as 'no rights' locks out every ordinary member.

No unique key on (user_id, role), deliberately. Two MODERATOR rows for one account with different scopes are the normal way to say 'moderates #feuerwehr, and everything in community Y' — a unique key would forbid exactly the case the scope model exists for. Legacy's duplicates, which carried no scope and meant nothing, are collapsed by the migration into one row.

Resolution order is the whole of the 'default roles cannot be overwritten' rule: RoleNames first, roles second. A row created before a default role of the same name existed stops being reachable the day that release ships, which is the intended direction — the code wins.

An unknown name is ignored with a warning, the same policy types/RoleNames.json declares. An older binary must survive a database written by a newer one, and an account whose only row is unknown falls back to USER rather than to nothing.
Renaming a created role rewrites this column for every holder, in the transaction that does the rename — see db/roles.json.
The scope hangs off the assignment, in user_role_scopes: not off the role, which is shared and reusable, and not off the account, which may hold two assignments that reach differently.

No JSON in a text column any more. visible_creation_groups, with its '*all' and '*untagged' sentinels, becomes rows in user_role_scopes under the creation_group dimension — '*untagged' as the reserved target_id 0, '*all' as the absence of rows.
The rights an account actually holds are not in this table. They come from the role: from code for a default role, from role_rights for a created one — see Architecture.md, Auth, and ../rights.json.
created_at and updated_at are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json.

Identifiers are uint64 throughout. Legacy is inconsistent here — users.id is int unsigned while referrer_id, contribution_link_id and publisher_id, which point at it, are bigint unsigned. A foreign key narrower than its target truncates silently in C, so gradido2 uses one width everywhere.

Written through role.assign, role.unassign and role.setScope, which address the assignment by id. The account-addressing routes they replace — user.setRole, creationGroup.get/setModeratorScope — are deprecated and must not be used to write this table once a second assignment can exist.
